title: Interleave, by Hec Labs — Cross-Domain Practice Scheduler
shortDescription: A cross-domain practice scheduler that tells multi-skill learners which skill to practice next, and for how long, by scoring every skill with a utility function over memory decay, desirable-difficulty urgency, cognitive fatigue, and prerequisite readiness.
problemStatement: People learning several unrelated skills at once (e.g., music + a language + programming) have no tool that optimizes across domains. Anki and FSRS tell you when to review a card; none of them decide which skill to work on next, or for how long. The self-regulated-learning literature shows learners systematically mis-schedule themselves — preferring blocked practice and trusting fluency illusions — so the scheduling decision itself is the unmet need.
myRole: Solo founder. Designed the utility-maximization model and switching policy, specified the closed-form v1 and the v2/v3 learned-model roadmap, and grounded every mechanism claim in a structured reading of the memory, interleaving, and knowledge-tracing literature.
technologiesUsed: LLM-based content extraction (skill graph + prerequisite DAG)
Planned v3: inductive R-GCN (two-relation graph neural network)
solutionApproachDescription: Interleave scores every skill each tick with U_i = 1[reachable] * (alpha*Urgency - beta*Fatigue + gamma*Readiness - lambda*Interference), and switches skills only when a rival beats the current one by a hysteresis margin delta — so session length is emergent, not a fixed timer. Urgency uses a SATURATING desirable-difficulty curve (flat at maximum for overdue skills, avoiding the death spiral a symmetric Gaussian would cause). Fatigue is modeled across four processing channels (logical, verbal, visual, fine-motor) as a leaky integrator. v1 ships fully closed-form with zero trained parameters and perfect cold-start; its real obligation is the append-only logging spine that becomes the training set for a learned decay model (v2) and, eventually, a graph neural network that models cross-skill transfer (v3).

impactSummary.overall: Interleave is in early development (v1). Its intended contribution is to make the cross-domain scheduling decision — which unrelated skill to practice next, and for how long — that no existing spaced-repetition or study tool addresses, while holding a high bar for scientific honesty about which mechanisms are validated versus novel.

details: A single answer to 'what should I practice next?' across unrelated domains, replacing ad-hoc self-scheduling that the research shows is systematically biased.
Emergent session structure tuned by one interpretable parameter (the hysteresis margin), rather than rigid fixed-length study blocks.

An honest cross-domain design: the benefit is claimed via forced spacing, contextual-interference-style variability, and channel-level fatigue relief — NOT the classic discrimination-based interleaving effect, which requires confusable categories that unrelated domains lack (Brunmair & Richter, 2019).
A logging spine built from day one so that novel components (the fatigue model, cross-domain transfer coefficients) can be empirically tested rather than assumed.

A version sequence gated by data, not preference: closed-form v1, linear Half-Life Regression at ~5-10k logged reviews, and a two-relation inductive GNN only once it beats calibrated HLR on a time-split evaluation.
Open-core intent: the algorithms and research are meant to be open, with a hosted service funding the infrastructure.

impactSummary.specialNotes: Scientific-honesty disclaimer is a brand pillar: components with no direct empirical validation (the four-channel fatigue model, skill-level decay extrapolation, cross-domain transfer) are explicitly flagged as novel and instrumented for testing, not presented as established results.
